ideas: Physics uses SI units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), newton (N), joule (J), watt (W), amp (A), volt (V), ohm (Ω).
Prefixes make numbers bigger or smaller: kilo (k) = × 1000, mega (M) = × 1 000 000, giga (G) = × 1 000 000 000.
Common conversions: cm → m ÷ 100 · g → kg ÷ 1000 · minutes → s × 60 · hours → s × 3600 · kJ → J × 1000 · mA → A ÷ 1000.
Area and volume: cm² → m² ÷ 10 000 · cm³ → m³ ÷ 1 000 000.
Standard form: 3 400 000 = 3.4 × 10⁶ and 0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴. Use the ×10ˣ button on the calculator.
Always convert to SI units BEFORE you put numbers into an equation.
words: The standard unit used in physics equations (m, kg, s, J …).
Letter in front of a unit that multiplies it, e.g. k = 1000.
A number written as A × 10ⁿ, where A is between 1 and 10.

example.q: Convert 450 g to kg and 2.5 kJ to J.

qs: Convert 35 cm to metres.
Convert 2.4 kW to watts.
Convert 3 minutes to seconds.
Convert 750 g to kilograms.
Convert 5 mA to amps. Give your answer in standard form.
Convert 4.2 MJ to joules.
Convert 600 nm to metres in standard form.
Convert 2 hours to seconds.
watch: Sense check: a length in metres is a SMALLER number than the same length in cm.
Don't convert things that are already in SI units (e.g. kg, m/s).

ideas: The Physics Equations Sheet is given in the exam. Questions that say 'Write down the equation that links…' can be answered from it.
Six steps every time: 1) write the equation, 2) convert units, 3) substitute the numbers, 4) rearrange, 5) calculate, 6) add the unit.
Substitute BEFORE rearranging. You get a method mark for correct substitution even if the answer goes wrong.
Rearranging: if something is multiplied, divide both sides by it. If something is divided, multiply both sides by it.
P = E ÷ t can become E = P × t or t = E ÷ P.
For a square: Ek = ½mv² → v² = 2Ek ÷ m → v = √(2Ek ÷ m).
Use brackets on the calculator when dividing by more than one number, e.g. 2400 ÷ (2 × 4200).
words: The quantity on its own on the left, e.g. P in P = E/t.
Replace the letters with the numbers from the question.

example.q: A 2000 W heater transfers 600 000 J of energy. How long was it on?

qs: V = IR. Current = 0.5 A, resistance = 12 Ω. Find V.
V = IR. V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω. Find I.
Ep = mgh. m = 2 kg, g = 9.8 N/kg, h = 5 m. Find Ep.
Ep = mgh. Ep = 490 J, m = 10 kg, g = 9.8 N/kg. Find h.
Ek = ½mv². Ek = 400 J, m = 8 kg. Find v.
watch: Equation triangles cause errors. Substitute into the equation exactly as it is written on the sheet.
Don't round in the middle of a calculation. Round only the final answer.

ideas: Energy stores: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal (internal), chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear.
Energy is transferred between stores by a force moving (mechanical work), an electric current (electrical work), heating, or waves (light, sound).
A system is an object or group of objects. In a closed system the total energy stays the same: energy is never created or destroyed.
Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv². Doubling the speed gives FOUR times the kinetic energy.
Gravitational potential energy gained when lifted: Ep = mgh, with g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
Work done: W = Fs (force × distance moved along the line of the force). 1 J = 1 N moved through 1 m.
Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store, so things warm up.
Falling with no air resistance: Ep lost = Ek gained, so mgh = ½mv². Mass cancels, so the final speed doesn't depend on mass.
words: An object or group of objects being studied.
Energy transferred when a force moves an object.
Energy can be transferred, stored or dissipated, but never created or destroyed.

example.q: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from 1.8 m. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving when it hits the ground?
steps: This all becomes kinetic energy: Ek = 8.82 J

qs: A 1200 kg car moves at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
A 60 kg climber climbs 25 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained.
A box is pushed with a force of 40 N for 3 m. Calculate the work done.
A cyclist doubles their speed. What happens to their kinetic energy?
It becomes 4 times bigger (because Ek depends on v²).
Describe the energy transfers when a bow fires an arrow straight up.
Elastic potential (bow) → kinetic (arrow) → gravitational potential as it rises. Some energy goes to the thermal store of the air because of air resistance.
watch: Kinetic energy is NOT mass × speed. Remember the ½ and the square.
When naming energy transfers, say how the energy changes or moves, not just the names of the stores.

ideas: Elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring: Ee = ½ke².
k is the spring constant (N/m). e is the extension in METRES: new length − original length.
This equation only works up to the limit of proportionality.
Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = E ÷ t, or P = W ÷ t. 1 watt = 1 joule per second.
Two motors lifting the same load the same height do the same work, but the more powerful one does it faster.
words: How stiff a spring is. Bigger k = harder to stretch.
How much longer the spring is than its original length.
Energy transferred per second, in watts (W).

example.q: A spring with k = 40 N/m is stretched by 5 cm. How much elastic potential energy does it store?

qs: k = 200 N/m, e = 0.1 m. Find Ee.
A spring stretches from 12 cm to 18 cm. k = 50 N/m. Find the energy stored.
A motor transfers 3600 J in 2 minutes. Find its power.
A 1.5 kW heater is on for 10 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?
A spring stores 2.5 J and has k = 500 N/m. Find the extension.
watch: Use the extension, not the total length.
Square the extension. This was the most common mistake in 2025.
Convert minutes to seconds and kW to W.

ideas: Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (or use power instead of energy).
The answer is a decimal between 0 and 1. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage.
Nothing can be more than 100% efficient.
Wasted energy is usually dissipated (spread out) to the surroundings as thermal energy, where it is less useful.
Ways to reduce wasted energy: lubrication (less friction), thermal insulation, streamlining.
Thermal conductivity: the higher it is, the faster energy is transferred through a material by conduction.
A house cools more slowly if its walls are thicker and have lower thermal conductivity.
words: The fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred.
Spread out to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy.
How quickly a material transfers energy by conduction.

example.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and transfers 350 J usefully. Find its efficiency.

qs: A lamp is supplied with 60 J and gives out 12 J as light. Find its efficiency.
A device is 0.25 efficient. The input is 2000 J. How much is useful?
A kettle has an input power of 2000 W and a useful output power of 1800 W. Find its efficiency.
Explain why lubricating a bike chain makes the bike more efficient.
It reduces friction, so less energy is wasted as thermal energy and more is transferred usefully to kinetic energy.
Give two ways to reduce energy loss from a house.
Any two: loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing, thicker walls, materials with low thermal conductivity.
watch: Useful goes on TOP. If your efficiency is bigger than 1, you've put it upside down.
Saying something 'saves energy' or 'wastes no energy' scores nothing. Say less energy is wasted.

ideas: Specific heat capacity (c): the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. Unit: J/kg °C.
ΔE = m c Δθ. Δθ is the temperature CHANGE (final − starting temperature).
Water has a high specific heat capacity (about 4200 J/kg °C), so it takes a lot of energy to heat.
Required practical method: measure the mass of the block on a balance. Put a heater and a thermometer in the holes. Wrap the block in insulation.
Record the starting temperature. Turn the heater on and measure the energy supplied with a joulemeter (or use E = V × I × t). Record the final temperature after, say, 10 minutes.
Calculate c = E ÷ (m × Δθ).
Some energy heats the surroundings, so the measured value of c is usually TOO HIGH. Insulation reduces this.

example.q: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg °C)

qs: 0.5 kg of aluminium (c = 900 J/kg °C) is heated by 20 °C. Find the energy needed.
12 600 J heats 0.3 kg of water (c = 4200). Find the temperature rise.
A 1 kg block gains 9000 J and warms by 20 °C. Find c.
Why is the value of c from the practical usually higher than the true value?
Some energy is transferred to the surroundings, so more energy is measured than actually went into the block.
Name three measuring instruments used in this practical.
Any three: balance, thermometer, joulemeter (or ammeter and voltmeter), stopwatch.
watch: Use the temperature CHANGE, not the final temperature.
In the 6-mark method question, say how each measurement is taken, including the mass.

ideas: Independent variable: the one you change. Dependent variable: the one you measure. Control variables: the ones you keep the same.
Accurate: close to the true value. Precise: repeat readings are close together.
Resolution: the smallest change an instrument can show, e.g. 1 mm on a ruler.
Repeatable: the same person gets similar results. Reproducible: someone else gets similar results.
Random error: readings vary unpredictably (e.g. reaction time). Reduce it by repeating and taking a mean.
Systematic error: every reading is wrong by the same amount, e.g. a zero error or always reading the scale from the same wrong angle.
Anomaly: a result that doesn't fit the pattern. Leave it out of the mean.
Uncertainty = range ÷ 2.

Thermal insulators practical: wrap identical beakers of hot water in different materials (or numbers of layers). Measure the temperature every minute for 10 minutes. Keep the starting temperature and volume of water the same.
words: An instrument that doesn't read zero when it should.
Reading a scale from an angle instead of at eye level.

example.q: A time is measured three times: 12.1 s, 12.4 s, 12.3 s. Find the mean and the uncertainty.

qs: A ruler always reads 2 mm too long. What type of error is this?
Systematic error (a zero error).
In the insulation practical, the number of layers is changed. Name the dependent variable and two control variables.
Dependent: the temperature drop after a set time. Controls: starting temperature, volume of water, type of material, time, beaker size.
Why do scientists repeat readings?
To spot anomalies and reduce the effect of random errors by taking a mean.
A thermometer is marked every 1 °C. What is its resolution?
Readings: 4.2, 4.5, 4.4, 6.9. Which is the anomaly and what is the mean?
watch: 'Human error' never scores. Name the actual error, e.g. reaction time or parallax.
Don't mix up precision, accuracy and resolution.

ideas: Non-renewable (will run out): coal, oil, gas (fossil fuels) and nuclear fuel (uranium).
Renewable (replaced as fast as it is used): solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, waves, geothermal, biofuel.
Fossil fuels: reliable and give lots of energy on demand, but release carbon dioxide (global warming) and sulfur dioxide (acid rain).
Nuclear: no carbon dioxide while running and very reliable, but makes radioactive waste and is expensive to shut down.
Wind and solar: no fuel cost and no carbon dioxide while running, but unreliable because they depend on the weather and daylight.
Hydroelectric: reliable and starts quickly, but flooding valleys destroys habitats.
Tidal: predictable, but affects habitats and there are few suitable places.
Geothermal: reliable, but only possible in a few places.
Biofuel: called carbon neutral because the plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.
Transport mostly uses oil (petrol and diesel). Heating mostly uses gas and electricity.
words: Will not run out; replaced as fast as it is used.
Takes in as much CO₂ as it releases.

example.q: Compare solar power and wind power. (2 marks)
steps: Similarity: both are renewable and release no carbon dioxide while running.
Difference: solar only works in daylight, but wind turbines can work at night.
example.a: One similarity and one difference, about both resources.

qs: Name two renewable resources that are reliable.
Any two: tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal (biofuel also accepted).
Why is wind power unreliable?
The wind doesn't always blow.
Give one advantage of nuclear power over coal.
No carbon dioxide is released while it runs (or: more reliable fuel supply, less fuel needed).
Why is biofuel described as carbon neutral?
The plants absorb carbon dioxide while they grow, which balances the carbon dioxide released when burned.
Give one disadvantage of hydroelectric power.
Flooding valleys destroys habitats (or: few suitable sites).
watch: For 'compare', always give a similarity AND a difference.
'It will run out' is too vague. Say non-renewable resources are finite and can't be replaced.

ideas: Learn the circuit symbols: cell, battery, switch, lamp, fuse, resistor, variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter, diode, LED, LDR, thermistor.
Current: the rate of flow of charge, in amps (A). Charge Q = I × t, in coulombs (C).
Potential difference (pd or voltage): the energy transferred per unit of charge, in volts (V).
Resistance: how much a component opposes the current, in ohms (Ω). V = I × R.
An ammeter goes in series. A voltmeter goes in parallel, across the component.
In a single loop, the current is the same everywhere.
words: Energy transferred per coulomb of charge.

example.q: A current of 300 mA flows through a component with 12 V across it. Find its resistance.

qs: A current of 2 A flows for 30 s. How much charge flows?
120 C passes a point in 1 minute. Find the current.
V = 9 V, R = 18 Ω. Find the current.
I = 0.2 A, R = 50 Ω. Find the pd.
How are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected?
Ammeter in series. Voltmeter in parallel, across the component.
watch: Convert mA to A and minutes to seconds.
Don't swap the ammeter and the voltmeter in circuit diagrams.

ideas: SERIES: the current is the same through every component. The pd of the supply is shared between components. Total resistance R = R₁ + R₂.
PARALLEL: the pd across each branch equals the supply pd. The total current is the sum of the branch currents. The total resistance is LESS than the smallest single resistor.
Adding resistors in series increases the total resistance because the current has to pass through each one.
Adding a resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance because it gives the current another path, so more current flows overall.
Wire resistance practical: clip crocodile clips to a wire at different lengths (e.g. every 10 cm). Measure V and I each time and calculate R = V ÷ I.
Plot resistance against length. You get a straight line through the origin: resistance is directly proportional to length.
Keep the current low, because a hot wire has a higher resistance.
words: Components in one loop, one after another.

example.q: A 4 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are in series with a 12 V battery. Find the current.

qs: A 9 V battery is in series with a lamp and a resistor. The pd across the lamp is 5 V. What is the pd across the resistor?
Two parallel branches carry 0.3 A and 0.5 A. What is the total current?
Two lamps are in parallel with a 6 V supply. What is the pd across each lamp?
6 V
Explain why adding a resistor in parallel lowers the total resistance.
It gives the current an extra path, so the total current increases for the same pd, which means the total resistance is lower.
Why should the current be kept low in the wire resistance practical?
A large current heats the wire, which increases its resistance and makes the results inaccurate.
watch: Be careful which rule goes with which circuit. In 2025, over 80% of students scored zero on this.
'Increase the resistance' alone isn't enough when asked how. Say 'use the variable resistor'.

ideas: Fixed resistor (at constant temperature): a straight line through the origin. Current is directly proportional to pd, and resistance stays the same.
Filament lamp: an S-shaped curve. As the current increases, the filament gets hotter, its ions vibrate more and its resistance increases.
Diode: current flows in one direction only. It has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
LDR: resistance decreases as light intensity increases. Used in automatic night lights.
Thermistor: resistance decreases as temperature increases. Used in thermostats.

I–V practical: put the component in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor, with a voltmeter across the component. Change the pd with the variable resistor and record I and V. Reverse the supply to get negative values.
words: A component where current is directly proportional to pd at constant temperature.
A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature.

example.q: On an I–V graph, a component has a current of 0.3 A at 6 V. Find its resistance at that point.

qs: What happens to the resistance of a filament lamp as the pd increases? Why?
It increases, because the filament gets hotter.
What happens when the pd across a diode is reversed?
Almost no current flows, because the resistance is very high.
A thermistor is in a fire alarm. What happens to its resistance as the temperature rises?
It decreases.
Why does a fixed resistor's I–V graph pass through the origin?
When the pd is zero the current is zero, and current is directly proportional to pd.
At night, what happens to the resistance of an LDR?
It increases (less light).
watch: For a diode, the key idea is that current flows in one direction only.
Don't say an LDR or thermistor 'gets more resistant' without saying the condition (light or temperature).

ideas: Electrical power: P = V × I, or P = I² × R.
Energy transferred: E = P × t, or E = Q × V.
Power ratings are in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW).
The energy transferred depends on the power and how long the appliance is on.
A large current heats wires (P = I²R). This is why the National Grid uses a low current.
words: The energy an appliance transfers per second.

example.q: A kettle on 230 V mains takes a current of 10 A for 2 minutes. How much energy does it transfer?

qs: V = 12 V, I = 2 A. Find the power.
I = 3 A, R = 4 Ω. Find the power.
A 2 kW heater is on for 30 minutes. Find the energy transferred.
50 C of charge moves through a pd of 6 V. Find the energy transferred.
A 1.2 kW appliance on 230 V runs for 5 minutes. How much charge flows?
watch: Convert kW to W and minutes to seconds before substituting.
Remember to square the current in P = I²R.

ideas: Direct current (dc) flows in one direction, e.g. from a cell. Alternating current (ac) keeps changing direction.
UK mains electricity is ac at 230 V and 50 Hz.
Plug wires: live is brown (230 V), neutral is blue (about 0 V), earth is green and yellow (0 V, a safety wire).
The live wire is dangerous even when a switch is off. Touching it makes a current flow through your body to earth, giving an electric shock.
If the live wire touches a metal case, a large current flows down the earth wire. This melts the fuse and cuts off the supply.
National Grid: power station → step-up transformer (very high pd) → transmission cables → step-down transformer → homes at 230 V.
Why a high pd? For the same power, a higher pd means a lower current. A lower current means less energy is wasted heating the cables, so the system is more efficient.
For a transformer: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.

example.q: A step-up transformer changes 25 000 V to 400 000 V. The primary current is 800 A. Find the secondary current.

qs: What colour is the live wire and what is its pd?
Brown, 230 V.
What is the frequency of UK mains electricity?
50 Hz
Why does the National Grid use step-up transformers?
To increase the pd and reduce the current, so less energy is lost heating the cables.
Explain how the earth wire and fuse protect someone.
If the live wire touches the metal case, a large current flows through the earth wire, the fuse melts and the circuit is broken, so the case is not live.
Why is touching the live wire dangerous?
There is a large pd between the wire and earth, so a current flows through your body: an electric shock.
watch: Saying 'the case becomes live' isn't enough. Say it causes an electric shock.
Don't mix up pd and current when explaining transformers.

ideas: Rubbing two insulators together transfers ELECTRONS from one to the other by friction.
The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The one that loses electrons becomes positively charged.
Only electrons move. Protons never move.
Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. This is a non-contact force.
A charged object has an electric field around it. The field is stronger closer to the object.
Field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. Around a charged sphere they are straight lines going out radially.
A spark happens when the pd between a charged object and earth is big enough for electrons to jump across the air gap.
words: The region around a charged object where another charge feels a force.
Connecting an object to the ground so charge can flow away safely.

example.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain why.
steps: Friction between the rod and the cloth…
…transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod.
The rod gains electrons, so it is negative. The cloth loses electrons, so it is positive.
example.a: Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod.

qs: After rubbing, what charge does the cloth have?
Positive, equal in size to the rod's negative charge.
Two negatively charged balloons are brought close. What happens?
They repel.
Describe the electric field lines around a positively charged sphere.
Straight lines pointing radially outwards from the sphere.
Why does a spark jump from a charged object to an earthed object?
The pd is very large, so electrons move across the air gap.
Why are fuel tankers earthed when refuelling?
To stop charge building up, which could cause a spark and ignite the fuel.
watch: Never say protons or positive electrons move. Only electrons move.
Draw at least three field lines with arrows, not bar-magnet style lines.

ideas: Density ρ = m ÷ V, in kg/m³ (or g/cm³). 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Solid: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating. Liquid: close together, random arrangement, moving past each other. Gas: far apart, random, moving fast.
Gases are least dense because the particles are far apart.
Changes of state are physical changes: they are reversible and mass is conserved.
Density practical, regular object: measure length, width and height with a ruler, volume = l × w × h. Measure mass on a balance.
Irregular object: lower it into a full displacement (eureka) can, or a measuring cylinder. The volume of water displaced equals the object's volume.
Liquid: put a measuring cylinder on a balance, zero it, add a measured volume of liquid and read the mass.
words: The water pushed out of the way equals the object's volume.

example.q: A stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water rises from 50 cm³ to 72 cm³. The stone's mass is 66 g. Find its density.

qs: A 2 kg object has a volume of 0.0025 m³. Find its density.
A block is 5 cm × 4 cm × 2 cm and has a mass of 120 g. Find its density.
Ice has a density of 920 kg/m³. Find the mass of 0.5 m³ of ice.
Why are gases less dense than solids?
The particles are much further apart.
Why is it better to use a displacement can for an irregular stone than a ruler?
Its shape is irregular, so you can't calculate the volume from measurements.
watch: Check whether the units are g and cm³ or kg and m³, and don't mix them.
Write the density equation correctly. Some students misquoted it in 2022.

ideas: Internal energy = the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Heating either raises the temperature (particles' kinetic energy increases) OR changes the state (particles' potential energy increases), not both at once.
Specific latent heat (L): the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. E = m × L.
Latent heat of fusion: solid ↔ liquid. Latent heat of vaporisation: liquid ↔ gas.
On a heating curve, sloping parts show the temperature rising (use E = mcΔθ). Flat parts show a change of state (use E = mL), with constant temperature.
words: Total kinetic + potential energy of the particles.
Energy to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change.

example.q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C? (L = 334 000 J/kg)

qs: 0.2 kg of boiling water turns to steam. L = 2 260 000 J/kg. Find the energy needed.
3 kJ melts 0.01 kg of wax. Find the specific latent heat.
Why does the temperature stay the same while ice melts?
The energy breaks the bonds between particles, increasing their potential energy, not their kinetic energy.
What is the difference between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat?
SHC: energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C. SLH: energy to change the state of 1 kg with no temperature change.
What happens to the internal energy of water as it is heated?
It increases.
watch: During a change of state, KINETIC energy stays the same and POTENTIAL energy changes. In 2025, only 3% got full marks for this.
Don't mix up specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.

ideas: Gas particles move randomly at high speed. When they collide with the container walls they exert a force. Pressure = force per unit area.
Heating a gas at constant volume: particles move faster, so they hit the walls MORE OFTEN and with MORE FORCE. The pressure increases.
At constant temperature, p × V = constant. Squash a gas into a smaller volume and particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises.
Doing work on a gas (e.g. pumping up a bike tyre) increases its internal energy, so its temperature rises.
words: Pressure × volume stays the same at constant temperature.

example.q: A gas at 100 kPa has a volume of 2 m³. It is compressed to 0.5 m³ at constant temperature. Find the new pressure.

qs: Explain why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated in a sealed container. (3 marks)
The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They collide with the walls more often and with more force, so the force per unit area (pressure) increases.
A gas at 150 000 Pa has a volume of 0.02 m³. Its pressure rises to 300 000 Pa at constant temperature. Find the new volume.
Why does a bike pump get warm when you use it?
Work is done on the gas, which increases its internal energy, so the temperature rises.
Why does a gas exert a pressure on its container?
Particles collide with the walls, exerting a force on them.
watch: Say collisions with the WALLS. 'More collisions between particles' scores nothing.
Mention both: collisions are more frequent AND each collision has more force.

ideas: An atom has a tiny positive nucleus (protons and neutrons) with electrons in shells around it. The atom's radius is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; the nucleus is about 10 000 times smaller.
Proton: charge +1, mass 1. Neutron: charge 0, mass 1. Electron: charge −1, almost no mass.
Atomic number = number of protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

History of the model: solid spheres → plum pudding (a ball of positive charge with electrons in it) → Rutherford's alpha scattering → nuclear model → Bohr's electron shells → Chadwick found the neutron.

Alpha scattering: most alpha particles went straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space. A few were deflected, so the nucleus is positive. Very few bounced back, so the mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

Alpha (α): 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Most ionising, stopped by paper, a few cm in air. Beta (β): a fast electron from the nucleus. Stopped by a few mm of aluminium. Gamma (γ): an electromagnetic wave. Least ionising, reduced by thick lead or concrete.
Nuclear equations: alpha decay → mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta decay → mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma → no change.
words: Same number of protons, different number of neutrons.
Knocks electrons off atoms, turning them into ions.
An atom that has lost or gained electrons.

example.q: Uranium-238 (atomic number 92) decays by alpha emission. What is the new nucleus?

qs: Carbon-14 has 6 protons. How many neutrons does it have?
Why did most alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil?
Most of the atom is empty space.
Radium-226 (atomic number 88) emits an alpha particle. Give the mass and atomic numbers of the new nucleus.
Mass 222, atomic number 86 (radon).
Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) decays by beta emission. What does it become?
Nitrogen-14: mass 14, atomic number 7.
Which radiation is most ionising, and what stops it?
Alpha. Stopped by paper (or a few cm of air).
What is an alpha particle made of?
2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus).
watch: An alpha particle is a helium NUCLEUS, not a helium atom.
In beta decay the atomic number goes UP by 1.

ideas: Radioactive decay is random: you can't predict which nucleus will decay next.
Activity = the rate of decay, in becquerels (Bq). A Geiger–Müller tube measures the count rate.
Half-life: the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei (or the activity) to halve.
After 1 half-life ½ is left, after 2 → ¼, after 3 → ⅛, after 4 → 1/16.
From a graph: find the starting value, halve it, and read across and down to find the time.
Irradiation: being exposed to radiation from a source outside the object. The object does NOT become radioactive.
Contamination: radioactive atoms get onto or into an object, which keeps being exposed until they are removed.
Inside the body, alpha is most dangerous (most ionising). Outside the body, beta and gamma are more dangerous because alpha can't get through the skin.
words: Time for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve.
Unwanted radioactive atoms on or in an object.
Exposure to radiation; the object doesn't become radioactive.

example.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 3 days. What is its activity after 9 days?

qs: The activity falls from 256 000 Bq to 16 000 Bq. How many half-lives is this?
The half-life is 5 years. How long does it take for the activity to fall from 1200 Bq to 300 Bq?
1200 → 600 → 300 is 2 half-lives = 10 years
What fraction of the nuclei is left after 3 half-lives?
⅛
What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
Contamination: radioactive atoms get on or into the object. Irradiation: the object is exposed to radiation from outside but doesn't become radioactive.
Why is an alpha source most dangerous inside the body?
Alpha is the most ionising, and inside the body it is right next to living cells, which it can damage.
watch: Answer the question asked: '4 half-lives', not the number you divided by (16).
'Exposure' alone isn't enough to define irradiation.

ideas: Background radiation comes from natural sources (rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays) and man-made sources (fallout from weapons tests and nuclear accidents, medical uses). Dose is measured in sieverts (Sv).
Medical tracers: a gamma emitter with a short half-life is injected or swallowed and detected outside the body.
Radiotherapy: gamma beams or implanted sources kill cancer cells.
Nuclear fission: a large unstable nucleus (uranium-235 or plutonium) absorbs a neutron, splits into two smaller nuclei, and releases 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
The released neutrons can cause more fissions: a chain reaction. In a reactor, control rods absorb neutrons to control it. An uncontrolled chain reaction is a nuclear explosion.
Nuclear fusion: two LIGHT nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus. Some mass is converted to energy. Fusion powers the stars and needs very high temperatures and pressures.
words: A large nucleus splits into two smaller ones.
Two light nuclei join to make a heavier nucleus.
Neutrons from one fission cause further fissions.

example.q: Describe the process of nuclear fission. (4 marks)
steps: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron.
The nucleus becomes unstable and splits into two smaller nuclei.
Two or three neutrons are released, along with gamma rays and energy.
These neutrons can go on to cause further fissions (a chain reaction).
example.a: Absorb neutron → splits → 2–3 neutrons + energy → chain reaction.

qs: Name two natural sources of background radiation.
Any two: rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays (from space), food and drink.
What is the purpose of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
They absorb neutrons, controlling the rate of the chain reaction.
Define nuclear fusion.
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
Why do medical tracers use gamma emitters with short half-lives?
Gamma passes out of the body to the detector, and a short half-life means the patient receives a smaller dose.
What would happen if a chain reaction were uncontrolled?
Energy would be released very rapidly, causing a nuclear explosion.
watch: Fusion needs 'light' or 'lighter' nuclei. 'Collide' alone scores nothing.
Don't mix up fission (splitting) and fusion (joining).

Today: questions 1 to about half way. Set a timer for 50 minutes.
Quiet place, no notes, calculator, ruler, equations sheet.
Spend about 1 minute per mark. If you get stuck, move on and come back.
Don't mark it yet. That's next session.
Do the second half of the June 2024 Paper 1H, 50 minutes.
Then mark the whole paper with the mark scheme. Be strict: only give a mark if your answer matches.
Add up the score and enter it in the Past papers tab.
Write the 5 biggest mistakes in the Past papers tab, e.g. 'forgot to convert cm to m'.
Look up which session covers each mistake and redo its practice questions.
Open the Past papers tab and read the mistakes you wrote down for both practice papers.
Redo only the questions where you lost marks. Use the mark scheme to check.
If a topic keeps coming up, go back to that session and redo its practice questions.
Read through the Exam tips tab.
Speed drill: 10 calculations from different sessions, using only the equations sheet. Aim for under 2 minutes each.
Pack for the mock: black pens, pencil, ruler, protractor, scientific calculator.
Have a calm evening. You've done the work.
When the marked mock papers come back, go through each question.
For every lost mark, write down the topic and the reason (didn't know it, misread the question, unit error, vague wording).
Count which topics lost the most marks. These go first in the new plan.
Share the list of lost marks so the plan can be rebuilt for the real exams starting 10 May.
Weakest topics go first; topics already rated 4 or 5 get quick recap sessions only.
Keep the same routine: 25-minute blocks, one session at a time.
Scalar: size only (speed, distance, mass, energy, time). Vector: size AND direction (velocity, displacement, force, acceleration, momentum).
Vectors are shown by arrows: the length shows the size and the arrow shows the direction.
Contact forces: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force, upthrust. Non-contact forces: gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force.
Weight W = m × g. Weight is a force in newtons (N); mass is in kg. g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Weight acts at the centre of mass.
Resultant force: the single force that has the same effect as all the forces together. Same direction: add. Opposite directions: subtract.
If the resultant force is zero, the forces are balanced.
Free-body diagram: a dot or box with a labelled arrow for each force acting on it. Longer arrow = bigger force.
Forces at an angle: draw them tip-to-tail to scale. The resultant goes from the start of the first arrow to the end of the last.
words: The overall force on an object.
The point where the weight seems to act.

example.q: A car has a driving force of 2000 N forwards and a total resistive force of 1400 N. Find the resultant force.

qs: Calculate the weight of a 65 kg person. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
Forces of 30 N to the right and 12 N to the left act on a box. Find the resultant force.
30 − 12 = 18 N to the right
Is mass a scalar or a vector? Is weight?
Mass is a scalar. Weight is a vector (it's a force).
Name two non-contact forces.
Any two: gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic.
A book rests on a table. Describe the forces on it.
Weight acts downwards; the normal contact force from the table acts upwards. They are equal, so the resultant is zero.
Forces of 3 N east and 4 N north act on an object. Find the size of the resultant.
Draw them tip to tail (or use Pythagoras): √(3² + 4²) = 5 N
watch: On free-body diagrams, draw arrows from the object, label each force, and make equal forces equal length.
Gravity is not a contact force. Weight is the force due to gravity.

ideas: Work done W = F × s. Work done = energy transferred.
To stretch, squash or bend an object, more than one force must act on it.
Elastic deformation: the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. Inelastic deformation: it doesn't.
Hooke's law: F = k × e. The extension is directly proportional to the force, up to the limit of proportionality.
On a force–extension graph this is a straight line through the origin. The gradient is the spring constant k. A curve at the end means the limit of proportionality has been passed.

Required practical: hang the spring from a clamp with a ruler beside it. Measure the original length. Add 1 N weights one at a time and measure the length each time. Extension = length − original length.
Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax error. Wear goggles in case the spring snaps.
words: The point after which force and extension are no longer proportional.
A straight line through the origin: double one, the other doubles.

example.q: A force of 6 N stretches a spring by 4 cm. Find the spring constant.

qs: k = 25 N/m and F = 5 N. Find the extension.
Explain the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation.
Elastic: the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. Inelastic: it stays permanently changed.
A force–extension graph curves at the top. What does this show?
The limit of proportionality has been exceeded.
A trolley is pushed with 50 N for 12 m. Find the work done.
How can you tell from a graph that force and extension are directly proportional?
It is a straight line that passes through the origin.
watch: 'As force increases, extension increases' is not enough for 'directly proportional'. Say it's a straight line through the origin.
Use extension, not length, and convert cm to m.

ideas: Moment of a force M = F × d (in N m). d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force.
Balanced object: total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment.
Levers and gears transmit turning effects. A longer lever (bigger d) needs less force for the same moment. A small gear turning a big gear makes it turn slower but with a bigger moment.
Pressure p = F ÷ A, in pascals (Pa). 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Pressure in a liquid p = h × ρ × g. It increases with depth and with density, and acts in all directions.
Upthrust: pressure is bigger at the bottom of an object than the top, giving an upward force. An object floats if the upthrust equals its weight, which happens if it is less dense than the liquid.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height, because there is less air above and the air is less dense.
words: The turning effect of a force.
The point an object turns around.
Upward force from a fluid on a submerged object.

example.q: A child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot of a see-saw. How heavy must a child 1.5 m from the pivot on the other side be to balance it?

qs: A 20 N force acts 0.3 m from a pivot. Find the moment.
A 500 N force acts on 0.25 m². Find the pressure.
Find the pressure from water 10 m deep. (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)
Why is it easier to undo a nut with a longer spanner?
The force is further from the pivot, so you get a bigger moment for the same force.
Why does a boat float?
The upthrust from the water equals the boat's weight.
watch: To increase a moment, say increase the force OR increase the distance from the pivot. Don't just say 'make the lever longer'.
Convert cm² to m² before calculating pressure.

ideas: Distance is a scalar. Displacement is a vector: the straight-line distance in a given direction.
Speed is a scalar. Velocity is speed in a given direction.
Typical speeds: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s, sound in air about 330 m/s.
Distance = speed × time (s = v × t).
Acceleration a = Δv ÷ t, in m/s². A negative acceleration is a deceleration.
Distance–time graph: the gradient is the speed. A flat line means the object is stationary. A curve means the speed is changing (draw a tangent to find the speed at one moment).
Velocity–time graph: the gradient is the acceleration. The AREA under the graph is the distance travelled. A flat line means constant velocity.
words: Distance in a straight line, with a direction.
How steep a line is: change up ÷ change across.

example.q: A car accelerates steadily from rest to 12 m/s in 6 s. How far does it travel?
steps: On a velocity–time graph this is a triangle

qs: A runner covers 1200 m in 4 minutes. Find the average speed.
A car goes from rest to 20 m/s in 8 s. Find its acceleration.
A v–t graph shows a constant 10 m/s for 30 s. How far does it travel?
What does a horizontal line on a distance–time graph mean?
The object is stationary.
A runner does one 400 m lap and finishes where they started. Give the distance and the displacement.
Distance 400 m. Displacement 0 m.
watch: On a velocity–time graph, distance is the AREA, not the reading. In 2023, 34% scored zero by using distance = speed × time.
Read the scales carefully before reading values off a graph.

ideas: For steady (uniform) acceleration: v² − u² = 2 a s. u = starting velocity, v = final velocity, s = distance.
Near Earth, a freely falling object accelerates at about 9.8 m/s².
Falling object, step by step: at first only weight acts, so it accelerates.
As speed increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force decreases and the acceleration decreases.
When air resistance equals weight, the resultant force is zero and the object falls at a constant speed: terminal velocity.
When a parachute opens, air resistance becomes bigger than weight, so the skydiver decelerates to a new, lower terminal velocity (larger surface area).
words: The maximum, steady speed of a falling object, when forces are balanced.

example.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 100 m. Find its final speed.

qs: A car slows from 30 m/s to rest over 45 m. Find its deceleration.
0 − 30² = 2 × a × 45 → −900 = 90a → a = −10 m/s² (deceleration of 10 m/s²)
A stone is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Find its speed (a = 9.8 m/s²).
Explain why a skydiver reaches terminal velocity. (3 marks)
As speed increases, air resistance increases. The resultant force (weight − air resistance) decreases. When air resistance equals weight, the resultant force is zero, so speed stays constant.
Why does opening a parachute lower the terminal velocity?
A bigger area means more air resistance, so forces balance at a lower speed.
watch: Gravity doesn't increase as you fall. It's the air resistance that changes.
Remember to square-root at the end, and don't forget u² if the object didn't start from rest.

ideas: Newton's first law: if the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps moving at the same velocity.
Inertia: the tendency of an object to stay at rest or keep moving at the same velocity.
Newton's second law: F = m × a. Acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass.
Newton's third law: when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on EACH OTHER (same type of force, acting on different objects).
Acceleration practical: a trolley on a bench is pulled by masses hanging over a pulley. Light gates (or a stopwatch and ruler) measure its acceleration.
To change the force but keep the total mass constant, move masses from the trolley onto the hanger.
words: Tendency to keep doing what it's doing.

example.q: A 1500 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s². Find the resultant force.

qs: A 20 N resultant force acts on a 4 kg mass. Find the acceleration.
A 600 N resultant force gives an acceleration of 3 m/s². Find the mass.
A swimmer pushes on the pool wall. Use Newton's third law to explain how she moves away.
She pushes on the wall; the wall pushes back on her with an equal and opposite force, which pushes her away.
A car moves at a steady speed. Compare the driving force and the resistive forces.
They are equal (resultant force zero, Newton's first law).
In the acceleration practical, why keep the total mass constant when changing the force?
So that only one variable (force) changes, making it a fair test.
watch: Don't just state Newton's laws. Apply them to the example in the question.
Third-law pairs act on DIFFERENT objects, so they don't cancel out.

ideas: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Thinking distance: the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (typically 0.2–0.9 s). Increased by higher speed, tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions.
Braking distance: increased by higher speed, worn brakes, worn tyres, wet or icy roads, more mass.
When braking, friction between the brake pads and the wheel does work, transferring kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes. Very large decelerations can overheat the brakes or cause a skid.
Momentum p = m × v (kg m/s). It is a vector.
Conservation of momentum: in a closed system, total momentum before = total momentum after.
Force = rate of change of momentum: F = m Δv ÷ Δt.
Airbags, seatbelts, crumple zones and helmets INCREASE THE TIME taken to stop. This reduces the rate of change of momentum, so the force on the person is smaller.
words: Time between seeing a hazard and pressing the brake.

example.q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Find their speed.

qs: Find the momentum of a 70 kg runner moving at 8 m/s.
A 0.4 kg ball goes from rest to 20 m/s in 0.05 s. Find the force.
A driver's reaction time is 0.6 s at 20 m/s. Find the thinking distance.
Explain how an airbag reduces injury in a crash. (3 marks)
It increases the time taken for the person to stop. This reduces the rate of change of momentum, so the force on the person is smaller.
Give two factors that increase braking distance.
Any two: higher speed, worn tyres, worn brakes, wet or icy road, greater mass.
watch: 'Cushions the person' or 'force is reduced' alone don't score. Link longer time → smaller rate of change of momentum → smaller force.
Don't mix up reaction time (a time) with thinking distance (a distance).

ideas: Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
Transverse waves: oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer, e.g. light and all EM waves, ripples on water, S-waves.
Longitudinal waves: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions, e.g. sound and P-waves. Sound needs a medium to travel through.
Amplitude: maximum displacement from the rest position. Wavelength (λ): distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next.
Frequency (f): number of waves passing a point per second, in hertz (Hz). Period T = 1 ÷ f.
Wave speed v = f × λ.

Waves practical: in a ripple tank, measure the wavelength across several waves with a ruler and count the waves passing in 10 s for frequency. On a vibrating string, measure the wavelength from the loops and read the frequency from the signal generator.
words: Oscillations at right angles to the direction of travel.
Oscillations parallel to the direction of travel.
Where the particles in a longitudinal wave are squashed together.

example.q: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz and travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Find its wavelength.
steps: v = f × λ → λ = v ÷ f

qs: f = 50 Hz, λ = 0.04 m. Find the wave speed.
Sound travels at 340 m/s. Find the wavelength of a 170 Hz note.
A wave has a frequency of 4 Hz. Find its period.
Compare transverse and longitudinal waves. (2 marks)
Similarity: both transfer energy. Difference: transverse oscillate at right angles to the direction of energy transfer, longitudinal oscillate parallel to it.
A duck on a pond bobs up and down as ripples pass. Why doesn't it move along with the waves?
Waves transfer energy, not the water (matter) itself.
watch: A 'compare' question needs a similarity, not just differences. In 2025, about half the students missed this.
Wavelength is a FULL wave, not half of one.

ideas: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line at 90° to the surface).
Specular reflection: from a smooth surface, in one direction. Diffuse reflection: from a rough surface, scattered.
Refraction: a change in direction when a wave changes speed as it crosses a boundary at an angle.
Light entering glass slows down and bends TOWARDS the normal. Leaving glass, it speeds up and bends away. Along the normal there's no change in direction.
Wavefronts: one end of the wavefront reaches the boundary first and slows down first, so the wavefront turns.
Frequency stays the same when a wave refracts; wavelength changes.

Refraction practical: place a glass block on paper and draw around it. Shine a ray from a ray box, mark the rays with crosses, remove the block, draw the normal and measure the angles with a protractor. Repeat for different angles of incidence.
Human hearing: 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is partly reflected at boundaries, so echo times give distances (scans, finding cracks). Distance = speed × time ÷ 2.

Seismic waves: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through solids and liquids. S-waves are transverse and travel through solids only. S-waves don't reach the far side of the Earth, so the outer core must be liquid.
words: A line at 90° to a surface.
Change of direction due to a change of speed.

example.q: An ultrasound pulse returns 0.0002 s after it was sent. The speed in the material is 1500 m/s. How deep is the boundary?

qs: The angle of incidence on a mirror is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
Light passes from air into glass at an angle. What happens to its speed and direction?
It slows down and bends towards the normal.
What is the range of human hearing?
20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz).
Why can't S-waves be detected on the opposite side of the Earth?
S-waves can't travel through liquids, and the outer core is liquid.
Explain refraction using wavefronts.
One end of the wavefront crosses the boundary first and changes speed first, so the wavefront changes direction.
watch: Measure angles from the NORMAL, not from the surface.
Don't mix up reflection and refraction. Many did in 2023.
'Human error' doesn't score in practical questions.

ideas: Electromagnetic (EM) waves are transverse and all travel at the same speed in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Order, longest wavelength to shortest: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma. Frequency and energy increase in that order.

Uses: radio (TV and radio broadcasts), microwaves (satellite communication, cooking), infrared (heaters, thermal cameras, remote controls), visible light (fibre optics), ultraviolet (energy-efficient lamps, sun tanning), X-rays and gamma (medical imaging and treatment).
Dangers: UV can cause skin to age and skin cancer. X-rays and gamma are ionising, so they can damage cells and cause cancer.
X-ray images: bones absorb X-rays, soft tissue lets them through.
Radio waves can be made by oscillating currents in a circuit, and can induce a current in a receiving aerial.

Infrared practical: fill a Leslie cube with hot water and measure the infrared from each face with a detector at the same distance. Matt black is the best emitter and absorber; shiny silver is the worst.
A perfect black body absorbs all the radiation falling on it and is the best emitter. Earth's temperature depends on the balance between radiation absorbed and emitted.
words: The family of EM waves, ordered by wavelength.
UV, X-rays and gamma: can damage cells.

example.q: Put these in order of increasing frequency: X-rays, radio, visible light.

qs: Which EM waves have the longest wavelength?
Radio waves.
Which EM waves are used for satellite communication?
Microwaves.
Give two dangers of ultraviolet radiation.
Skin ageing and skin cancer (also eye damage).
Which surface of a Leslie cube emits the most infrared?
Matt black.
Why do bones show up on an X-ray image?
Bones absorb X-rays, but soft tissue lets them pass through.
watch: Mnemonic for the order: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns.
Don't confuse UV (ultraviolet) with ultrasound.

ideas: Convex (converging) lens: parallel rays meet at the principal focus. It can make real or virtual images.
Concave (diverging) lens: rays spread out as if coming from the principal focus. Its image is always virtual, upright and smaller.
Focal length: the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
Real image: rays actually meet, so it can be shown on a screen. Virtual image: rays only appear to come from it, so it can't be put on a screen.
Magnification = image height ÷ object height (no units).
Ray diagram for a convex lens: a ray parallel to the axis bends through the principal focus; a ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on. Where they meet is the image.
Visible light: red has the longest wavelength, violet the shortest.
An object looks red because it reflects red light and absorbs the other colours. White reflects all colours; black absorbs all. A filter lets through only its own colour.
words: Where parallel rays meet (or seem to come from).
An image that can't be projected onto a screen.
How many times bigger the image is.

example.q: An object 2 cm tall forms an image 6 cm tall. Find the magnification.

qs: What is the difference between a real and a virtual image?
A real image can be projected onto a screen (rays meet). A virtual image can't (rays only seem to come from it).
Which type of lens is a magnifying glass?
Convex (converging).
Why does a red apple look red in white light?
It reflects red light and absorbs all other colours.
What colour does a red object look under blue light?
Black (no red light to reflect).
What type of image does a concave lens always make?
Virtual, upright and smaller.
watch: Write 'virtual', not 'not real' or 'fake'.
Use a ruler and put arrows on rays in ray diagrams.

ideas: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Magnetic field lines go from north to south and are closest together (strongest) at the poles.
A permanent magnet makes its own field. An induced magnet only becomes a magnet when it's placed in a magnetic field, and loses most of it when removed.
Magnetic materials: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always attraction.
Use a plotting compass to map a field. The Earth has a magnetic field, which makes a compass point north.
A current in a wire makes a circular magnetic field around it. The field is stronger with more current and closer to the wire.
Solenoid (coil of wire): the field is like a bar magnet's, strong and uniform inside. Adding an iron core makes a stronger electromagnet.
Motor effect: a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (except when the wire is parallel to the field). F = B × I × l.
Fleming's left-hand rule: thuMb = Motion (force), First finger = Field (N to S), seCond finger = Current (+ to −).
DC motor: forces on the two sides of the coil act in opposite directions, so it turns. The split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn so it keeps turning the same way.
Loudspeaker: an alternating current in the coil makes it and the cone move in and out, making sound waves.
words: Becomes a magnet only when in a magnetic field.
Force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.

example.q: A 0.5 m wire carrying 3 A sits at right angles to a 0.2 T magnetic field. Find the force on it.

qs: A 0.1 m wire carrying 2 A feels a force of 0.06 N. Find the magnetic flux density.
Give two ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
Any two: more current, more turns on the coil, add an iron core.
What is an induced magnet?
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field.
Why does a motor's coil keep turning in the same direction?
The split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn.
Give two ways to make a motor spin faster.
Any two: more current, stronger magnet, more turns on the coil.
watch: Don't confuse motors (current → movement) with generators (movement → current).
Say 'stronger magnet', not 'bigger magnet'.

ideas: Generator effect: when a wire moves relative to a magnetic field (or the field around it changes), a potential difference is INDUCED across it. If the circuit is complete, a current flows.
The induced current makes its own magnetic field, which opposes the movement that caused it.
To increase the induced pd: move faster, use a stronger magnet, or use more turns on the coil.
Alternator: a coil turns in a magnetic field. Slip rings and brushes keep the connections the same, giving alternating current (ac).
Dynamo: uses a split-ring commutator, so the output is direct current (dc). It never goes negative, but it rises and falls.
Microphone: sound waves vibrate a diaphragm attached to a coil in a magnetic field, inducing an alternating current that matches the sound.
Transformer: two coils on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary coil makes a changing magnetic field in the iron core, which induces an alternating pd in the secondary coil.
Iron is used because it is easily magnetised (not because it conducts electricity).
Step-up transformer: more turns on the secondary. Vp ÷ Vs = np ÷ ns. For a 100% efficient transformer: Vp × Ip = Vs × Is.
words: A pd caused by a changing magnetic field.
Keep a generator's connections the same, giving ac.
Swaps the connections every half turn.

example.q: A transformer has 200 turns on its primary coil and 1000 on its secondary. The input pd is 12 V. Find the output pd.

qs: A transformer changes 230 V to 11.5 V. The primary coil has 2000 turns. How many turns does the secondary have?
Why does a transformer have an iron core?
Iron is easily magnetised, so it carries the changing magnetic field to the secondary coil.
Why won't a transformer work with direct current?
dc gives a steady magnetic field. It must be changing to induce a pd.
Give two ways to increase the pd from a generator.
Any two: turn it faster, use a stronger magnet, use more turns of wire.
What is the difference between an alternator and a dynamo?
An alternator uses slip rings and gives ac; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator and gives dc.
watch: This is the hardest topic. In 2023 only 2% got full marks explaining a dynamo. Learn the basics and move on.
Say a pd is 'induced', not 'created'.

ideas: Our solar system: one star (the Sun), 8 planets, dwarf planets such as Pluto, natural satellites (moons) and artificial satellites. It is part of the Milky Way galaxy.
The solar system formed from a cloud of dust and gas (a nebula) pulled together by gravity.
Life cycle of a star: nebula → protostar (gravity pulls it together and it heats up) → main sequence star (hydrogen fuses into helium).
A main sequence star is stable because the outward force from fusion energy balances the inward pull of gravity.
A star like the Sun: red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf. A much bigger star: red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.
Fusion in stars makes elements up to iron. Heavier elements are made in supernovas, which spread elements through the universe.

Orbits: gravity pulls towards the centre. In a circular orbit the speed stays the same but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes. That means the object is accelerating towards the centre. A smaller orbit needs a faster speed.
Red-shift: light from distant galaxies has a longer observed wavelength (shifted towards red). More distant galaxies have bigger red-shifts, so they are moving away faster. The universe is expanding.
This supports the Big Bang theory: the universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region and has been expanding ever since.
words: The long, stable stage of a star's life.
Increase in the observed wavelength of light from galaxies moving away.
Theory that the universe began from a tiny, hot, dense point and expanded.

example.q: Explain why a satellite in a circular orbit is accelerating even though its speed is constant. (3 marks)
steps: The direction of the satellite keeps changing.
Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity.
A changing velocity means it is accelerating (towards the Earth, due to gravity).

qs: Give the stages in the life of a star the size of the Sun.
Nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf → black dwarf.
What keeps a main sequence star stable?
The outward force from fusion balances the inward force of gravity.
Where are elements heavier than iron made?
In supernovas.
What is red-shift and what does it tell us?
The observed wavelength of light from distant galaxies is longer. It shows galaxies are moving away, so the universe is expanding.
How does red-shift support the Big Bang theory?
More distant galaxies are moving away faster, so the universe is expanding, which means it must once have been much smaller, hotter and denser.
watch: Galaxies don't emit longer wavelengths. The wavelength we OBSERVE is longer. Only 6% got full marks for red-shift in 2023.
Give a reason why a star changes stage, not just the names of the stages.

ideas: Find the June 2024 Paper 2H and the equations sheet (see Resources).
